bank_runs_page_description: Banks lend out your deposits under fractional reserve banking. If too many people withdraw at once, banks can fail. Bitcoin is a full-reserve system — bank runs are impossible.
bank_runs_header: Bitcoin doesn't have bank runs, but your bank might.
bank_runs_what_p1: Banks don't hold your deposits in a vault. They lend your money out and invest it — that's called fractional reserve banking.
bank_runs_what_p2: If too many people try to withdraw at the same time, the bank doesn't have enough cash to pay everyone. That's a bank run — and it can cause banks to collapse entirely.
bank_runs_card_bank_reserve_detail: Since March 26, 2020, U.S. banks are required to hold 0% in reserves.
bank_runs_card_btc_reserve_detail: Every bitcoin exists on-chain — nothing is lent out.
bank_runs_svb_heading: Silicon Valley Bank: a real example

bank_runs_svb_p1_b: When those bonds lost value, SVB couldn't cover withdrawals. The bank was insolvent.
bank_runs_svb_p2: Thousands of businesses couldn't pay their employees. The FDIC stepped in — but that raised a bigger question: is your money actually safe?

bank_runs_fdic_p1: FDIC insurance protects deposits up to $250,000 per depositor. But the insurance fund is tiny compared to the total deposits it's supposed to protect.

bank_runs_card_btc_fdic_detail: Full-reserve system — no deposit insurance needed.
bank_runs_bitcoin_p1: Bitcoin is a full-reserve system. You're not depositing your money in a bank. You are your own bank. There's no lending out your money without your knowledge because you are the only one who can access your money.
bank_runs_bitcoin_p2: As long as you hold bitcoin in your own wallet — not on an exchange or wrapped in an ETF — bank runs are impossible.
bank_runs_bitcoin_p3: With Bitcoin, you're truly in control of your money.
